rules.why: G-1: the organisation name in a citation is a checkable property of the text, independent of capitalisation.

anchor.quote: Always use an initial capital for ‘the Treasury’ to show the difference from its generic reference.

parts.quote: The Treasury conducts itself to the highest standards.

tags.violation_condition: The government organisation referred to as ‘the Treasury’ is written with a lower-case ‘t’.

when: The reference is to the government organisation, not a generic treasury.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: the Treasury convention is the specific exception to the generic department-reference convention.

anchor.quote: Use initial capitals for the formal names of areas in a department or agency's organisational structure.

covers.quote: Don't use initial capitals for generic mentions of parts of the formal names.

parts.quote: The Budget Policy Division is part of Treasury’s Fiscal Group. The division coordinates the delivery of the Budget and other fiscal reports.

tags.violation_condition: A formal organisational-area name lacks its required capitals, or a generic reference to that area unnecessarily retains capitals.

when: The reference is to an area within a department or agency's organisational structure.
Generic mentions of parts of the formal name take lower case.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: formal and generic references to organisational areas are cases of one check.

anchor.quote: Use an initial capital letter for ‘federal’ when it forms part of a formal name.
anchor.suffix: Don’t capitalise it when it is

covers.prefix: it forms part of a formal name.
covers.quote: Don’t capitalise it when it is used as an adjective.

federal issues

tags.violation_condition: ‘Federal’ is lower case within a formal name, or is unnecessarily capitalised when used as an ordinary adjective.

when: Distinguish formal-name uses from ordinary adjectival uses of ‘federal’.
Normal sentence-initial capitalisation is not a violation.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: the formal-name and adjectival cases change the required casing of the same word.

anchor.quote: Use an initial capital for the word ‘federation’ only when referring to Australia’s Federation in 1901.

tags.violation_condition: ‘Federation’ is lower case when referring to Australia's Federation in 1901, or has an unnecessary capital when it does not refer to that event.

when: References derived from the 1901 event include Federation style architecture.
Normal sentence-initial capitalisation is not a violation.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: the historical referent determines which casing is required.

anchor.quote: Use an initial capital for the word ‘government’ if it is part of a formal name.

covers.prefix: if it is part of a formal name.
covers.quote: Use lower case everywhere else.
Use an initial capital for both words only when they occur together.

tags.violation_condition: ‘Government’ is lower case in a formal government name, or is unnecessarily capitalised in a generic or plural reference.

when: ‘Australian Government’ takes initial capitals when the two words occur together as the formal name.
Generic, adjectival and plural references to government take lower case.
Normal sentence-initial capitalisation is not a violation.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the Australian Government casing instruction is a specific case of the government-word check, not a second finding.

anchor.quote: Use initial capitals for the full names of:

covers.quote: government programs
treaties
protocols and similar agreements.

the Artesian Basin Initiative
the initiative

tags.violation_condition: A full or still-specific abbreviated name of a government program, treaty, protocol or similar agreement lacks its required capitals, or a generic reference unnecessarily retains capitals.

when: The name is for a government program, treaty, protocol or similar agreement.
Abbreviated names retain capitals only while remaining specific.
Generic references and generic abbreviations take lower case.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: full, specific abbreviated and generic names are conditions of one naming-capitalisation check.

anchor.quote: Use initial capitals for the formal and abbreviated titles of current heads of state.

covers.quote: You do not need to use capitals for generic references to the position or when referring to previous incumbents.

The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom chairs Cabinet meetings.
The Sultan of Oman comes from a dynasty of rulers. The Sultan met with the Prime Minister last week.

tags.violation_condition: The formal or abbreviated title of a current head of state or prime minister lacks its required initial capitals.

when: The section includes prime ministers as well as heads of state.
Capitals are not required for generic references to the position.
Capitals are not required when referring to previous incumbents.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: generic references and previous incumbents relax the capitalisation requirement; the permission is not a separate prohibition.

anchor.quote: Use initial capitals for these terms when referring to specific legislation:

covers.quote: Act
Ordinance
Regulation

Generic references to bills, regulations and ordinances take lower case.
All legislative references to Acts take initial capitals.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: specificity changes the casing check, with Acts as the explicit exception.

anchor.quote: Use initial capitals for the official titles of ministers and departmental secretaries.
anchor.suffix: Use lower case for generic refe

Apply this rule to the titles of other government office holders and department officials.

The Secretary of the Department of Social Services gave the opening address. Several secretaries attended the forum.
The Minister for Education announced the new policy. Education groups met with the Minister to present their views.
The Secretary of the Department of Social Services gave the opening address. Several Secretaries attended the forum.

tags.violation_condition: An official ministerial or departmental-official title lacks its required capitals, or a generic reference to such an office holder is unnecessarily capitalised.

when: This includes ministers, departmental secretaries and other government office holders and department officials.
Use the page's more specific checks for heads of state, institutional principals and parliamentary titles rather than flagging the same casing twice.
Generic references take lower case.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: formal versus generic references and the extension to other officials belong to one title-capitalisation check.

anchor.quote: Always use ‘for’ (not ‘of’) for a minister’s portfolio.

parts.quote: the Minister for Education
the Minister of Education

tags.violation_condition: A minister's portfolio is introduced with ‘of’ or another preposition instead of ‘for’.

when: The preposition connects a ministerial title to the minister's portfolio.
rules.why: G-1: portfolio prepositions are separate from capitalisation and from departmental-employment prepositions.

anchor.quote: Generally, use ‘of’ for anyone working at a department or agency.

parts.quote: Secretary of the Department of Health.
Secretary for the Department of Health

tags.specification: Apply this to title or affiliation constructions such as ‘Secretary of the Department of Health’, not to every ordinary sentence about someone working for an organisation. ‘Generally’ leaves exceptions unspecified.
tags.violation_condition: A title or affiliation connecting a person to their department or agency uses ‘for’ or another unsuitable preposition where ‘of’ is expected.

when: The construction identifies a person's departmental or agency affiliation.
A minister's portfolio follows the separate ‘for’ convention.
rules.why: G-1: this is a different title relationship and has a qualified recommendation, unlike the mandatory ministerial-portfolio wording.

anchor.quote: In many cases, you need to use initial capitals for the official titles of the principals and chief executives of Australian institutions.

covers.quote: Use lower case for most of these titles in general references that do not refer to a specific person.

examples.note: The departmental-secretary example also illustrates the preceding, more specific title rule.

parts.quote: the Chief Justice of the High Court of Australia
the Attorney-General
The Secretary of the Department of Social Services
the Vice-Chancellor and President of the University of Queensland
the Premier of New South Wales
the Chief Minister of the Northern Territory
The average salaries of vice-chancellors have reached a new high.
Several attorneys-general met to discuss the issue last week.
The premiers of New South Wales and Victoria met to discuss health reforms.

tags.specification: A reviewed title-and-exception list is needed: the page does not enumerate the exceptions implied by ‘in many cases’ and ‘most’. General references normally take lower case when they do not refer to a specific person.
tags.violation_condition: An institution principal's or chief executive's official title lacks capitals required for that title, or a general reference unnecessarily uses capitals.

when: The title belongs to a principal or chief executive of an Australian institution.
Ministerial and departmental-secretary titles are handled by their specific rule.
Titles covered by the heads-of-state or parliamentary-title guidance should not receive a duplicate finding.
Most general references that do not identify a specific person take lower case.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: official titles and general references are cases of one check; the manual's qualifications remain explicit.

anchor.quote: Use initial capitals for words in the formal name.

‘Territory’ is an exception when used for the Northern Territory

covers.suffix: Use lower case for generic refe

covers.quote: Use lower case for generic references.

tags.violation_condition: An Australian state or territory's formal name lacks its required capitals, a generic or plural state/territory reference is unnecessarily capitalised, or the semi-official Northern Territory name ‘Territory’ is incorrectly lower case.

when: The reference is to an Australian state or territory.
Generic and plural references take lower case.
‘Territory’ takes a capital when used as the semi-official substitute for ‘Northern Territory’, but not when used generically.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: formal, generic and plural uses share one casing check; the Northern Territory convention is an explicit exception.

member; members

tags.violation_condition: A formal parliamentary name or office-holder title lacks required capitals, a current member's formal title is incorrectly lower case, or a non-formal parliamentary term is unnecessarily capitalised.

Generic references and terms that are not formal titles take lower case.
Names and references to the houses themselves follow the more specific houses rule.
Normal sentence-initial capitalisation is not a violation.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.

anchor.quote: Always use initial capital letters to refer to:

tags.violation_condition: A formal parliamentary-house name or formal shortened name lacks its required capitals, or a generic or alternative house reference has casing inconsistent with the specified convention.

when: Formal names include the Senate, the House of Representatives and corresponding state and territory bodies.
Formal shortened names such as ‘the Assembly’ retain capitals.
The collective expression ‘houses of parliament’ is lower case.
House of Representatives references include ‘the House’ and ‘this House’, but ‘lower house’ and ‘people’s house’ are lower case.
Senate alternatives ‘this house’, ‘upper house’, ‘house of review’ and ‘states’ house’ are lower case.
The alternative-reference lists establish casing conventions, not an exhaustive ban on other descriptions.
Specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation may be an exception.
rules.why: G-2: formal names, shortened names and alternative house references are cases of the same house-reference casing check.
